name: Angyuan Ma

papers.title: F2F-AP: Flow-to-Future Asynchronous Policy for Real-time Dynamic Manipulation
papers.abstract: Asynchronous inference has emerged as a prevalent paradigm in robotic manipulation, achieving significant progress in ensuring trajectory smoothness and efficiency. However, a systemic challenge remains unresolved, as inherent latency causes generated actions to inevitably lag behind the real-time environment. This issue is particularly exacerbated in dynamic scenarios, where such temporal misalignment severely compromises the policy's ability to interpret and react to rapidly evolving surroundings. In this paper, we propose a novel framework that leverages predicted object flow to synthesize future observations, incorporating a flow-based contrastive learning objective to align the visual feature representations of predicted observations with ground-truth future states. Empowered by this anticipated visual context, our asynchronous policy gains the capacity for proactive planning and motion, enabling it to explicitly compensate for latency and robustly execute manipulation tasks involving actively moving objects. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly enhances responsiveness and success rates in complex dynamic manipulation tasks.

papers.title: WAM-STEP: Self-Improving World-Action Models Through Efficient Post-Training
papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) improve robot policies by predicting future visual consequences, but inference-time video prediction increases latency. Recent efficient WAMs avoid this cost by using the visual branch only during training and deploying an action-only policy. However, predicted futures remain an auxiliary loss and do not explicitly guide policy improvement. We propose WAM-STEP, an efficient post-training framework that turns the training-only visual branch of a WAM into an internal imagination module for self-improvement. WAM-STEP first calibrates the visual branch on mixed-quality policy rollouts to model policy-induced outcomes, using an action-conditioned preference loss to improve action-following future prediction. It then freezes the calibrated visual branch and optimizes the action branch using reward-scored imagined futures, with a policy-anchor baseline to stabilize group-relative updates. This enables efficient consequence-to-action feedback without introducing a separate world-model simulator or adding video generation at inference. On RoboCasa365, WAM-STEP improves the base policy from 20.7% to 24.0% average success. On two real-world tasks, WAM-STEP achieves 62.5% average success, outperforming the base policy by 20 points. These results show that training-time visual consequences can be internalized into stronger action-only robot policies.
